title: Not one book
hook: these texts don't combine into one scripture, and their communities would say so
tomorrow: you can't keep every book. which one goes home with you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel on one foot: one line, then go and learn. Each asks its own. Today, a bigger question: should all those asks be bound into one book?
screen: `EACH ASKS ITS OWN.` → `ONE BOOK, OR MANY?`

segments.voice: A playlist on shuffle will put a hymn next to a breakup song next to a podcast, and it all flows as one stream. It's tempting to read sacred books that way too. At the Parliament of Religions in Chicago, a Hindu monk, Swami Vivekananda, stood up and quoted a hymn from his own tradition: "As the different streams having their sources in different places all mingle their water in the sea," so, it goes on, the many paths all lead to the one Lord.
screen: `ONE STREAM ON SHUFFLE.` → `VIVEKANANDA IN CHICAGO.` → `STREAMS INTO ONE SEA.`

segments.voice: Two real views live inside this path. Let both speak. The first is the one sea. Its best case: it makes room for every seeker, it ends the fight over whose road is real, and it treats every honest search as leading home. Vivekananda taught it as Vedanta, a Hindu teaching, and a generous one. The second is separate shelves. Its best case: these books don't combine, and their own communities would say so. The Quran speaks of itself as a scripture from God. The Torah speaks of a covenant with a people. The Heart Sutra speaks of emptiness and never names a Creator. Bind them together and each loses what it actually says. Even the one-sea image, this side adds, isn't neutral ground; it's one tradition's teaching about the rest. Long before Chicago, the Indian emperor Ashoka carved an edict on rock with a third way between them. Honor other sects, it says. Restrain your speech. Whoever praises his own sect by running down others harms his own. Listen to one another's teaching. Concord, not one creed. Here's where this path lands, plainly: separate shelves. Honor each book the way its own people read it, and hold Vivekananda's sea as what it is, a Hindu teaching, worth loving on its own shelf.
screen: `VIEW ONE: THE ONE SEA.` · `VIEW TWO: THESE BOOKS DON'T COMBINE.` · `ASHOKA: HONOR, RESTRAIN, LISTEN.` · `EACH ON ITS OWN SHELF.` · then, large: `SEPARATE SHELVES.`

segments.voice: Picture a long wooden bookcase with a shelf for each book you met here: the Psalms, the Gita, the Analects, the Heart Sutra and the rest. Set each one on its own shelf in your mind, spine out, with a little space around it. Let them stand side by side without leaning on each other.
Not one book: these texts stand side by side, each in its own house, not bound into one.
Your line: separate shelves. Side by side, each in its own house, never stapled together. Until next time.

screen: `DAY 1494 COUNTS.` → `CLOSING THE READING · 2 OF 4.` → `TOMORROW: YOU CAN'T KEEP EVERY BOOK. WHICH ONE GOES HOME WITH YOU?`

howItsDone: People who read across traditions differ: some, following teachers like Vivekananda, see many paths to one goal; others keep each scripture within its own community's reading. Both views appear in interfaith settings.

fork.setup: you lean toward separate shelves. steelman the other side: what's the best case for Vivekananda's one sea?
options: it makes room for every seeker and ends the fight over whose road is real.
it proves that every religion teaches exactly the same thing.

fork.reveal: his image welcomes every path as leading to the one Lord: a real and generous view, and itself a teaching of one tradition.

what a scholar hears: Vivekananda's streams come from a Hindu hymn (the Shiva Mahimna Stotra); Ashoka's Rock Edict XII asks for concord and restraint in speech, not one creed.

chat.says: theo says all these books are one truth in different outfits. inés says that's rude to all of them. help
options: Both have a case, but 'one sea' is itself a Hindu teaching. Separate shelves honor each.
Theo's right. Every tradition teaches that they're all the same underneath.
Inés is right. Reading more than one tradition's book disrespects all of them.
chat.meaning: Vivekananda's 'streams into one sea' comes from a Hindu hymn; Ashoka asked people to honor and listen to each other's teaching without merging them.

tie.story: Vivekananda quoted a hymn of streams meeting in one sea; Ashoka's edict asked every sect to honor the others and restrain its speech.
tie.friend: Zoe can tell Theo and Inés she reads each book as its own people do, which is how she gets to love all of them.
tie.you: which book do you read through someone else's lens?

Vivekananda.meaning: a Hindu monk who taught Vedanta in the West

Vedanta.meaning: a Hindu school of thought on the one reality behind all

Ashoka.meaning: an ancient Indian emperor who carved edicts on rock

Heart Sutra.meaning: a short Mahayana Buddhist text on emptiness
